claims.claim: The de Havilland Comet was the world's first commercial jet airliner, entering BOAC scheduled service in May 1952.
claims.definition: first jet-powered aircraft to enter scheduled commercial passenger service
claims.authoritative_source: RAF Museum — 'Comet: the world's first jet airliner'
claims.notes: status stable; historical fact, not a living record

claims.claim: In 1954, Comets G-ALYP (10 January, BOAC Flight 781) and G-ALYY (8 April, SAA Flight 201) broke apart in flight at cruise altitude; the fleet was grounded.
claims.definition: in-flight structural breakups of intact, serviced aircraft, attributed by the inquiry to pressurization-cycle metal fatigue
claims.authoritative_source: Wikipedia — BOAC Flight 781; De Havilland Comet
claims.notes: both accidents in the Mediterranean; no survivors

claims.claim: The Comet cruised near 40,000 ft with a cabin pressure differential of about 8.25 psi — the fuselage works like a pumped balloon every flight.
claims.definition: pressure differential between cabin and ambient air at cruise altitude
claims.notes: modern airliners run similar differentials at similar altitudes

claims.claim: A circular opening in pressurized skin carries about 3x the far-field stress at its rim (the Kirsch factor); sharp corners concentrate stress well beyond that.
claims.definition: Kirsch (1898) solution: stress concentration factor K = 3.0 at the rim of a circular hole in an infinite plate under uniform tension; square corners with small radii exceed it substantially
claims.notes: textbook result; the qualitative corner comparison is what the diagram shows

claims.claim: In the RAE water-tank fatigue test, Comet fuselage G-ALYU burst after 3,057 pressurization cycles (1,221 real + 1,836 simulated flights), against a 10,000-cycle design life.
claims.definition: one pressurization cycle = one cabin pressurize/depressurize sequence; the test hull failed at under a third of its specified life
claims.authoritative_source: historicalrfa.uk — crash of BOAC Comet Yoke Peter; dh-aircraft.co.uk inquiry archive
claims.notes: the tank test reproduced the fatigue failure under controlled cycling

claims.claim: The fatal crack in G-ALYP was traced to a rivet hole at the rear ADF antenna window cutout — a square-cornered opening in the fuselage roof — not to the passenger windows.
claims.definition: per the official inquiry: fatigue crack initiation at the ADF antenna 'window' cutout, aggravated by punch riveting instead of the intended glued (Redux) joints
claims.measured_value: crack origin: ADF antenna window cutout, fuselage roof
claims.notes: V5 §18 honesty note: the popular 'square passenger windows' story is a simplification; the verified origin is the antenna cutout + rivet holes. The video keeps this precise.

claims.claim: The Comet redesign rounded every pressurized opening and thickened the skin; the Comet 4 entered service in 1958, and rounding every cutout became standard practice for pressurized aircraft.
claims.definition: post-inquiry design changes: generous radii on all openings (windows, doors, hatches, cutouts) to cut stress peaks; still standard on every pressurized airliner today
claims.measured_value: rounded openings + thicker skin; Comet 4 in service 1958
claims.authoritative_source: RAF Museum; Wikipedia — De Havilland Comet
claims.notes: engineering practice, not a record claim
